title: Arthur Samuel Coins 'Machine Learning' (1959)
explainer: The term 'machine learning' has a traceable birth: Arthur Samuel's 1959 IBM Journal paper on a checkers-playing program that improved its own play by adjusting the weights it used to evaluate board positions. Samuel's program is a good anchor for this lesson's vocabulary because it already contains, in miniature, the core idea the field's terms are built around: a program that gets better at a task from experience rather than from being handed new explicit rules. It's worth knowing the word has a specific origin rather than treating it as a label that has always existed.

title: The Dartmouth Workshop and the Coining of 'Artificial Intelligence' (1956)
explainer: The term 'artificial intelligence' didn't emerge gradually; John McCarthy coined it for a specific 1955 funding proposal, the 'Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence,' and it became the name of the 1956 workshop where McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon gathered a small group to study thinking machines. Knowing this grounds today's often-blurred AI/ML vocabulary (AI, ML, and deep learning are not synonyms, and each term was coined for a specific reason at a specific moment) in real history. McCarthy reportedly chose the name partly to sidestep the existing baggage of terms like 'cybernetics.'
